Central Vietnam Flood of 2019 Disrupted Gas & Water Utilities, Prompted Infrastructure Rethink

In the aftermath of the severe flooding that struck central Vietnam in October 2019, the Gas & Water Utilities sector has reflected on the widespread disruption it experienced and the lessons learned. Torrential rains, triggered by a tropical depression, caused the Thu Bon River to overflow and inundate several key facilities operated by utilities providers in Quang Nam and Da Nang provinces.

The flooding, which local meteorological officials described as the worst in a decade, forced temporary shutdowns at multiple water treatment plants and gas distribution nodes, leading to service interruptions for thousands of households and businesses. "Our Quang Nam water processing facility was inaccessible for 36 hours due to floodwaters rising over two meters," said Nguyen Van Hoang, Chief Operations Officer at Pacific Waterworks. "We activated our emergency supply protocols, but some areas experienced outages until we could restore access."

Gas transmission was also affected, with submerged pipelines and obstructed access routes delaying deliveries. VietGas Utility reported that landslides along the main highway added to the logistical challenges. "We had to halt gas deliveries to the southern districts for two days because our transport vehicles could not reach the depots," explained Tran Thi Minh, Operations Director at VietGas Utility.

The Vietnam Utilities Association estimated that total direct losses for the sector from the October 2019 floods reached VND 180 billion (approximately USD 7.7 million). "This event exposed vulnerabilities in our existing infrastructure, especially in flood-prone areas," said Tran Quoc Binh, spokesperson for the Association. "It underscored a pressing need for investment in more resilient facilities and emergency planning."

Analysts note that while utilities have since resumed normal operations, the events of 2019 have accelerated discussions around climate adaptation. "The 2019 floods were a wake-up call for the industry," commented Le Thi Lan, a sector analyst at Hanoi-based Mekong Insights. "Companies are now revisiting site selection and reinforcing critical assets, especially in regions that face recurring extreme weather."

Union representatives have also called for enhanced worker safety measures during natural disasters. "Ensuring employee safety in hazardous conditions is paramount," said Doan Huu Phuc, chairman of the Utilities Workers Union.

While the disruption is now in the past, industry leaders emphasize that the 2019 floods will have a lasting influence on future planning and investment in Vietnam's Gas & Water Utilities sector.
